articles.title: Fox News Poll: Nail-biter in Maine Senate race
articles.summary: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson are deadlocked at 49% in the Maine Senate race as Trump's job approval sits 25 points underwater in the state.
articles.body: Maine voters are in a negative mood this election season. Only 12% say their family is better off financially compared to two years ago, and more than 6 in 10 disapprove of President Donald Trump’s job performance, including 2 in 10 Republicans. FOX NEWS POLL: TEXAS SENATE RACE GALLOPING TOWARD A PHOTO FINISH A Fox News survey of Maine likely voters finds that mood weighs on Republican Sen. Susan Collins, as 53% are concerned she votes with Trump too much. By contrast, 46% are concerned Democratic challenger Troy Jackson is too liberal. FOX NEWS POLL: GENDER GAP AND POCKETBOOK PAIN SHAPE OHIO SENATE RACE Despite those views, the horse race shows the candidates tied, with Jackson and Collins at 49% apiece. All survey interviews were completed after the candidates’ Oct. 15 debate. Collins, who first won her seat about three decades ago, is seeking a sixth term. She’s the only GOP senator running for re-election this year from a state Trump lost in 2024 (by 7 points). In 2020, Collins won by nearly 9 points. Democrats view Maine as a must-win seat in their effort to take control of the Senate. When voters are asked about control of the U.S. Senate, 53% prefer a Democratic-led Senate vs. 45% who want the Republicans to remain in charge. While almost all Jackson supporters want Democratic control (96%), Collins supporters are more divided: 89% want a GOP-led chamber, but 9% prefer Democratic leadership. Collins will need to overcome the energy on the left, as far more Democrats (79%) than Republicans (61%) say they are extremely interested in the election, which explains why Jackson is ahead by 16 points among that group. He’s up by 4 points among those who say they are "certain" to vote, and also carries the one in five Mainers who have already cast a ballot by a decisive 40 points. On the other hand, a slim majority plans to vote on Election Day, and they favor Collins by 12 points. "Collins is no stranger to outrunning her party, but Democrats hold an 18-point enthusiasm advantage," says Mikaela Linder of Beacon Research, a Democratic polling firm that conducts the Fox News Poll with Republican Daron Shaw. "Trump’s job rating is 25 points underwater, and a majority strongly disapproves of him. Jackson has an opening if he can carry that momentum beyond his base and across the finish line." Views of the president’s performance are a problem for GOP candidates in Maine. Currently, 37% of voters approve of the job Trump is doing as president, while 62% disapprove, including 54% who strongly disapprove. The candidates’ personal favorability ratings are both underwater. Views of Jackson are negative by 2 points (47% favorable, 49% unfavorable), and by 4 points for Collins (47%-51%). Partisan vote choice varies distinctly across key groups. Voters under 45 favor Collins by 6 points, while those ages 45 and older prefer Jackson by 3. Women support Jackson by 5 points, while men back Collins by 4. The sharpest divide is education: Mainers with a college degree pick Jackson by 23 points, while Collins leads among those without a degree by 16. Collins is ahead among those living in rural areas by 7 points, while Jackson is the pick of the smaller number of suburban voters by 18 points. For comparison, in 2020, Collins won both the voters living in rural areas and those without a college degree by 18 points each. "Republicans appear to be struggling with White rural voters this cycle, and Maine is no exception," Shaw said. "GOP candidates desperately need these voters to show up, and need something like a 65-35 vote to overcome Democratic strength in urban areas." Party loyalty is roughly even as 9 in 10 of each candidate’s party faithful back them, and the small subgroup of independents favors Collins by 13 points. Both Jackson (92%) and Collins (90%) supporters have a high degree of vote certainty. In Maine’s gubernatorial race, Democrat Hannah Pingree leads Republican Bobby Charles by 10 points, 49% to 39%, while independent candidate Rick Bennett takes 9%. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Unlike Jackson, whose coalition backs Pingree almost unanimously (only 8% defect), nearly one in five Collins supporters (19%) peel off to either Bennett (11%) or Pingree (8%). Conducted October 16-20, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 1,689 Maine registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (226) and cellphones (1,035) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (428). Results based on the registered voter sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2 percentage points and for the subsample of 1,514 likely voters it is ±2.5 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education, and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Likely voters are based on a probabilistic statistical model that relies on past vote history, interest in the current election, intention to vote, age, education, race, ethnicity, and marital status. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100. Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ramaswamy controversy pits Trump, Vance against Ohio GOP establishment
articles.summary: The controversy over Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s mother is pitting President Trump and Vice President Vance against Ohio’s Republican establishment less than two weeks out from Election Day. A number of Ohio Republicans, including Gov. Mike DeWine and Sen. Jon Husted, have denounced the ad, which…
articles.body:
The controversy over Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his Democratic opponent Amy Acton’s mother is pitting President Trump and Vice President Vance against Ohio’s Republican establishment less than two weeks out from Election Day.

A number of Ohio Republicans, including Gov. Mike DeWine and Sen. Jon Husted, have denounced the ad, which features Acton’s mother insinuating her daughter has mental health issues. Acton’s brother later released a statement saying he and his sister have been estranged from their mother since Acton was 12 because their mother stayed married to the man who sexually abused Acton at a young age.

Still, Vance and Trump have offered ardent defenses of Ramaswamy.

Trump called DeWine a “RINO” — meaning “Republican in name only” — and said Ramaswamy “should keep it up” in a lengthy Truth Social post Thursday.

Vance said Wednesday he was “a little bit disgusted” with Republicans “whining” about the advertisement more than they are about Democrats.

Trump and Vance’s reactions stand in stark contrast from many members of Ohio’s Republican establishment.

“The Republicans who are being critical are largely anti-Trump Republicans or very establishment Republicans,” said one Ohio GOP strategist.

The same strategist noted the approach taken by Trump is emblematic of his political instinct to punch back and not back down.

“This is Trump’s attitude. Good, bad or indifferent. I don’t think I’ve ever heard him say the word I’m sorry,” the Ohio strategist said.

Husted, who was previously DeWine’s lieutenant governor, said in a statement to The Associated Press that he “would not have run” the ad. DeWine called on Ramaswamy to take down the ad while speaking with reporters, calling the spot “deeply, deeply troubling.”

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose (R) told ABC 6 in Columbus that his office was reviewing complaints over the ad, echoing Husted’s response about what he would do in such a situation.

“I will say that, you know, candidates will answer for their own ads, that, you know, I probably wouldn’t run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision,” LaRose told the local outlet.

Other former senior Ohio political figures are speaking out against the ad. Former Gov. John Kasich (R) told MS NOW there “is nothing appropriate about the ad.”

“Any claim of sexual abuse or anything that could lead to the discussion about that has no place in American politics,” Kasich said.

Former Sen. Rob Portman (R-Ohio), who Vance replaced in the Senate, said in an interview with Politico on Thursday that the ad “crosses the line” and should be taken down.

“It’s Ohio,” said Chris Johnson, an Ohio Republican strategist. “With candidates like DeWine or Husted, where they are just good, nice guys, they want to go out there and fight for their deeply held conservative values, but they do it in such a way that is very midwestern.”

“They’d much rather be talking about the issues or talking about who the Buckeyes play that weekend,” he added.

The fallout over the ad puts Husted, who has been on the receiving end of Trump’s praise in recent days, in an awkward position.

Husted is facing a formidable challenger in former longtime Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown (D). According to polling released earlier this week from the Cook Political Report, Brown leads Husted 49 percent to 43 percent. Cook has rated the race as a toss-up.

The incumbent senator was already facing a tough race against Brown, who is considered a staple in Ohio politics. While Husted has won statewide races before as lieutenant governor and as secretary of State, he was not elected to the Senate. Instead, he was appointed by DeWine to replace Vance when he became vice president.

Additionally, the national environment and state of the economy has proven to be another obstacle for Republicans running in tough races.

While the Cook Political Report rates the governor’s race as a toss-up, recent polling shows Ramaswamy trailing Acton. A Marist University poll released Tuesday showed Acton leading Ramaswamy by 7 points, while polling from the Cook Political Report showed her leading by 5 points.

Johnson said he was skeptical the ad, while emblematic of Trump and MAGA World’s style, would persuade undecided swing voters.

“Even if it is swinging for the fences, trying to finish strong down the stretch here, that’s not who you’re trying to convince,” Johnson said. “I worry that once people start looking into this story that it might backfire a little bit.”

Alex Triantafilou, chair of Ohio’s Republican Party, appeared to remain neutral in a social media post, saying he is for the leaders who can turn out voters.

“As State Party Chairman, here’s the score I will always keep: we laud, support, and appreciate those GOP leaders who help turn out our voters and proclaim the good policies and good government of the Republican Party. LET’S GO!” Triantafilou wrote.

The Republican National Committee (RNC), on the other hand, sided with Trump and Vance.

“As President Trump and Vice President Vance have stated, this manufactured outrage is a distraction from what this election is actually about: Amy Acton is too liberal for Ohio, and her far-left agenda would take the state backward,” RNC spokesperson Hunter Lovell said in a statement.

“Keeping Ohio red is a top priority for President Trump, which is why he’s visited the state twice this month with a third rally planned next week. Republicans are united behind Vivek Ramaswamy, who will always put Ohioans first, and help him defeat Liberal Amy Acton on November 3,” he continued.

Trump is slated to take his third visit to Ohio this month, underscoring the importance of both races.

Acton, who previously was not receiving the national attention she is now, has spoken out against the ad in interviews, calling it “despicable.”

On Thursday, her campaign sent out a fundraising appeal about Ramaswamy’s ad, citing Republican division over the spot.

“He’s stooped so low that even Republicans are calling him out,” Acton said in the fundraising email.

articles.title: Supreme Court says New Hampshire student IDs can’t be used to vote in November
articles.summary: In a win for Republicans, the court said a federal judge should not have changed the rules so close to the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — In a win for Republicans, the Supreme Court said Thursday that student IDs cannot be used in New Hampshire for the midterm elections. The justices granted an emergency request filed by the state, which had the backing of the Republican National Committee. The ballot in New Hampshire includes a closely watched Senate race that could play a key role in deciding control of the chamber. Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu is pitted against Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas for the seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. The brief court order said a federal judge should not have ordered a change in voting rules so close to the Nov. 3 election, citing existing precedent on that point. “Here, the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle,” the unsigned order said. Liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the sole dissenter. “I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes,” she wrote. While a state law restricting use of student IDs as a primary form of identification was already on the books, the decision means potential voters also cannot use them as backups when they seek to establish their identities. The dispute arises from a state law enacted in April that removed student IDs from the list of forms of identification that election officials would accept when someone requests a ballot. The measure was challenged by a nonprofit voting rights group called Coalition for Open Democracy, which argued that it unlawfully burdened the right to vote and discriminated against young voters. U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante declined to block the law, but on Oct. 2 he weighed in again, putting guidance from New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, on hold. Scanlan’s guidance said student IDs could not be used for any purpose when people seek ballots, which Laplante said went further than the law itself, which only barred them as a primary source of ID. A separate provision of state law allows people to establish their identities using other, unofficial forms of ID. It says people can use “any other evidence that reasonably establishes that it is more likely than not that the person is who they claim to be.” Under Laplante’s ruling, election officials could still take a student ID into account in trying to determine whether someone is a valid voter. The Boston-based 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put Laplante’s ruling on hold, prompting the state to ask the Supreme Court to intervene.

articles.title: Jackson says he’s ‘concerned’ about Georgia rural voter turnout
articles.summary: Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson (R) is sharing his concerns about rural turnout in his election, as early voting is underway across the Peach State. “I am concerned that rural Georgia still thinks we’re red and therefore they look at somebody like myself and my opponent and just say, ‘Well, there’s no comparison,’” Jackson said…
articles.body:
Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson (R) is sharing his concerns about rural turnout in his election , as early voting is underway across the Peach State.

“I am concerned that rural Georgia still thinks we’re red and therefore they look at somebody like myself and my opponent and just say, ‘Well, there’s no comparison,’” Jackson said at a campaign stop , according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

Early turnout figures, aggregated by nonpartisan election data site VoteHub, show Black voters turning out at high rates in the first few days of early voting. While Black voters will be critical to Democrats winning statewide, Jackson relies on rural Georgia to turn out in big numbers.

Jackson is running in a competitive race against former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D).

Georgia is traditionally a battleground state, but Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) has consistently led by wide margins in polls of his reelection bid. Bottoms is running far closer, but Democrats hope that a big win for Ossoff could pull Bottoms over the finish line.

A poll from the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and the University of Georgia released this week found Ossoff ahead by eight points, 48 percent to 40 percent, while Jackson led Bottoms by one point, 46 to 45.

Former President Obama will visit Georgia next week to campaign with Ossoff and Bottoms.

One area where Jackson has a significant advantage is in fundraising. As a billionaire and healthcare executive, Jackson has been able to self-fund a significant portion of his campaign throughout the primary and general election. Jackson has put over $100 million of his own money into the gubernatorial race and has significantly outspent Bottoms.

While Democrats are unlikely to match Jackson’s fundraising, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D), also a billionaire, donated $1 million to Bottoms’ campaign, Politico reported Tuesday.

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Bottoms a 56 percent chance of winning the Georgia gubernatorial contest.

articles.title: Supreme Court sides with GOP in New Hampshire student ID voting fight
articles.summary: Republicans asked the Supreme Court to block the use of student IDs as a backup form of voter identification in New Hampshire for the midterms.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court said New Hampshire can fully enforce a ban on voters using student IDs as a form of identification at the polls next month, a win for the Republican Party's effort to tighten voting procedures.

The court on Oct. 22 agreed to pause a lower court's ruling that a student ID is among the forms of identification that may be considered by poll workers if the voter lacks an approved government-issued ID.

The state's U.S. Senate race is among the contests that will decide whether Republicans keep control of that chamber after the midterm elections. The Republican National Committee had backed the state's unsuccessful emergency appeal to the Supreme Court .

Key midterm election races that will determine control of Congress

U.S. Senate, Alaska Dan Sullivan (R) vs. Mary Peltola (D) Incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is defending his seat against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman. Peltola would be the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate if she wins in November.

New Hampshire, controlled by Republicans, is among several states that have banned registered voters from using a student ID to verify their identity at the polls. A voting-rights group challenged the change as discrimination against younger voters and as an unconstitutional burden on their right to vote.

A federal judge in New Hampshire declined to block enforcement of the law as the case is litigated.

But the judge also said the new law had not changed the fact that a poll worker may accept or reject a student ID as a valid form of identification on a case-by-case basis through the state's "safety-valve" provision.

New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

Scanlan, a Republican, said the judge's Oct. 2 order injected uncertainty into the state's voting procedures less than three weeks before the election. He also said the judge wrongly interpreted the state's law.

Coalition for Open Democracy, the group challenging the law, said the judge correctly concluded that state officials failed to identify "any security or integrity concerns specific to student ID cards and why they are unique among other non-governmental forms of identification" that are allowed on a case-by-case basis.

The judge also found that the change had already kept one student from voting and could affect more because young voters may not have the government-issued IDs that are automatically accepted.

In the brief and unsigned opinion, the Supreme Court pointed to its previous rulings that federal courts should not alter rules on the eve of an election.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly disagree with that decision. She said the federal judge had not changed the rules but only corrected the secretary of state's misinterpretation of them.

"I respectfully dissent because − even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming − I would not disturb aclearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State'selectoral processes," she wrote.

U.S. Senate, Georgia Jon Ossoff (D) vs. Mike Collins (R) Incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is taking on GOP Rep. Mike Collins, a Trump-endorsed candidate, for a crucial seat in November. The race has captured national attention as Trump has personally attacked Ossoff, while Collins has been swept up in a House ethics investigation and faced questions about his son-in-law, a White nationalist influencer. (Ossoff: Jack Gruber, USA TODAY; Collins: Getty Images)

U.S. Senate, Iowa Josh Turek (D) vs. Ashley Hinson (R) Current GOP Sen. Joni Ernst decided not to run for a third term, setting up Iowa’s first open Senate race since 2014. Democratic State Rep. Josh Turek, a two-time gold medalist Paralympian, faces Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former TV anchor now in her third term in Congress. (Zach Boyden-Holmes, The Des Moines Register via USA TODAY Network)

U.S. Senate, Maine Susan Collins (R) vs Troy Jackson (D) Collins was seen as one of the GOP’s most vulnerable senators in 2026. But Democrats’ efforts to unseat her were complicated when their nominee Graham Platner dropped out of the race amid allegations of sexual assault. Jackson, the former Maine Senate president and logger, was picked to replace Platner. (Collins: Getty Images; Jackson: Reuters)

U.S. Senate, Michigan Abdul El-Sayed (D) vs. Mike Rogers (R) Running on a progressive platform, El-Sayed won a bruising primary that saw much of the Democratic party establishment back his opponent. Rogers, who served seven terms in the House, is making his second bid for a Senate seat after losing to Elissa Slotkin in 2024. (Abdul El-Sayed: Pool Photo; Mike Rogers: Jasper Colt, USA TODAY)

U.S. Senate, New Hampshire John E. Sununu (R) vs. Chris Pappas (D) Republicans are hoping that former Sen. John Sununu can flip the seat held by retiring Democrat Jeanne Shaheen. Sununu is endorsed by Trump and won the GOP primary over former Massachusetts Sen. Chris Brown. U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas is the Democratic nominee. (USA TODAY Network)

U.S. Senate, North Carolina Roy Cooper (D) vs. Michael Whatley (R) Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, a moderate who served two terms, faces off against former Republican National Chair Michael Whatley, a close Trump ally. (Reuters)

U.S. Senate, Ohio Jon Husted (R) vs. Sherrod Brown (D) Brown, who served three terms in the Senate before losing to Bernie Moreno in 2024, is making a bid to return to Washington in a special election for the final two years of JD Vance’s term. He faces incumbent Husted, who was appointed to fill the vacant Senate seat when Vance became vice president. (USA TODAY Network)

U.S. Senate, Texas Ken Paxton (R) vs. James Talarico (D) Ken Paxton, Texas’ state attorney general, ousted incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary after receiving Trump’s endorsement. He faces a stiff challenge from state Rep. James Talarico in what will be one of the most closely watched contests of 2026. (Getty Images)

articles.body:
Calley Means , a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a leader in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, resigned from the Trump administration Thursday, less than two weeks before the midterm elections.

© Kent Nishimura, Bloomberg via Getty Images

His departure signals a further divide of the unique coalition that helped propel President Trump to the White House.

Means said he is resigning “with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy.”

Means helped lead Health and Human Services initiatives around food policy , including an effort to change how companies disclose chemicals in food, remove artificial food dyes and ban soda and sugary drinks from the SNAP federal food assistance program.

Means was widely credited with introducing Trump and Kennedy , leading to Kennedy suspending his own presidential campaign and endorsing Trump.

But Means was reportedly growing disillusioned with the administration, frustrated over delays in implementing key pieces of the MAHA food agenda.

For instance, the White House over the summer teased a major announcement about defining ultra-processed foods, but that has yet to come to fruition amid major pushback from industry groups.

The MAHA base is increasingly at odds about the administration’s relationship to their core policy goals — eliminating pesticides and chemicals in the food supply and encouraging healthy eating by reducing reliance on ultra-processed foods.

A coalition of MAHA activists released a “scorecard” earlier this month, claiming the administration broke 85 percent of its promises to restrict pesticide use, promote healthier foods and break up special interests in Washington.

In a post on the social platform X, Means said that Kennedy and Trump “laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick,” and have made significant progress in the past two years.

“More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history – and I know this movement is just getting started,” he wrote.

Allison Schuster, a White House spokeswoman, said in an email: “We are grateful for Calley Means’ time in the Trump Administration. He has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement.”

articles.title: Trump advances two wind projects
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Trump advances two wind projects The Trump administration is advancing some wind projects after a court order required it to do so. © Joshua A. Bickel, Associated Press file A White House official said Thursday that an initial set of wind projects under Pentagon…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is advancing some wind projects after a court order required it to do so.

© Joshua A. Bickel, Associated Press file

A White House official said Thursday that an initial set of wind projects under Pentagon review have been released. The official said this represents two projects located in Maine and South Dakota.

The official said the Defense Department will keep evaluating wind projects on a case-by-case basis.

The official also described the move as clearing the path for a bipartisan energy bill in the Senate. That legislation — which is expected to cut down on barriers, including environmental laws for energy projects — is the result of a tenuous deal between Democrats and Republicans, and comes after significant ire from the left over the Trump administration’s moves to hold up renewable energy projects.

The advancement of the two projects comes after the administration earlier this year froze approvals for onshore wind projects, citing potential interference with doppler radars. A lawsuit earlier this year said at least 125 utility-scale projects in 25 states were impacted.

In August, a federal judge halted the Pentagon’s freeze as a case against it plays out. Earlier this week, organizations that sued over the department’s treatment of wind projects asked the court to take additional steps to enforce the order, saying the administration was failing to comply with it.

The move also comes as the Trump administration has taken other steps to hamper wind energy in recent weeks. It recently requested to reconsider previously approved permits for several offshore wind projects.

articles.title: Trump on Lewandowski probe reports: ‘I want my people to be honest’

articles.body:
President Trump said Thursday that he has “no idea” why the Justice Department is investigating Corey Lewandowski for misconduct, but that anyone working for him has to be honest.

Those that are not honest, Trump went on to say, will face the DOJ.

“I want my people to be honest, and if they’re not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted,” Trump told reporters before departing the White House in response to a question about a reported investigation of Lewandowski.

“I view it as if people are not honest, they’re stealing from me as president, they’re stealing from me,” he said. “So I want my people to be honest, and if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DOJ go and do whatever they have to do.”

The Justice Department is looking into a criminal referral from the Department of Homeland Security Inspect General, according to reports. The accusations include that he profited from his role.

The office has been examining contracting practices at the agency when Lewandowski was there.

Trump said he “will never do anything to stop a prosecution if somebody is dishonest.”

Lewandowski worked alongside former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who was ousted in March.

“Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity,” Lewandowski’s attorney Adam Trigg told NewsNation.

Lewandowski was Trump’s first campaign manager back in 2016 and played a role in his subsequent campaigns.

articles.title: Supreme Court rules NH can block voters from using student IDs
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled New Hampshire’s top election official can fully stop voters from using their student IDs when showing up to the polls in the midterms — a request backed by the Republican National Committee (RNC). A lower judge ruled officials had improperly gone further than a new state law placing restrictions on…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled New Hampshire’s top election official can fully stop voters from using their student IDs when showing up to the polls in the midterms — a request backed by the Republican National Committee (RNC).

A lower judge ruled officials had improperly gone further than a new state law placing restrictions on student IDs to get a ballot.

The judge said the state still needed to consider student IDs alongside other evidence when a voter lacks other ways to prove their identity.

The Supreme Court chastised the judge for intervening too close to November’s contests.

“New Hampshire has a responsibility to protect the integrity of its elections and ensure that election laws are applied as written,” New Hampshire Attorney General John Formella (R) said in a statement. “The Supreme Court’s decision is an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials. We will continue to defend New Hampshire’s election laws and the safeguards they provide.”

The high court has said such orders can cause voter confusion, known as the Purcell principle. The opinion points to the recent legal whiplash over Missouri’s redistricting as one recent example.

“Here, the District Court did not point to anything that would justify deviating from that principle,” the majority wrote in its unsigned, one-paragraph opinion.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson publicly dissented, saying the rule didn’t apply since the judge in New Hampshire was helping ensure the public received accurate information.

“When a federal court determines that material misrepresentations are being made about a State’s election rules, an injunction to prohibit that conduct does not contribute to public confusion, it prevents that very problem,” Jackson wrote.

It is not a final ruling in the litigation, and it could return to the Supreme Court after the midterms.

New Hampshire’s Senate race has emerged as a key state to watch in the battle for control of the upper chamber in November’s midterms, as Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas faces off against former Republican Sen. John Sununu to succeed the retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D).

New Hampshire’s emergency request to enforce its student ID guidance got the support of the RNC. It placed the blame on the plaintiffs, the Coalition for Open Democracy, saying they had delayed the proceedings.

“Months passed, and election season began, in the time that the Coalition waited,” the RNC’s lawyers wrote to the Supreme Court.

articles.title: NYC votes to end nearly 170-year-old horse carriage tradition as Trump blasts ban, drivers threaten lawsuit
articles.summary: The Transport Workers Union threatened federal court action after the New York City Council voted 40-7 to ban horse-drawn carriages by June 2028.
articles.body: The New York City Council voted Thursday to ban horse-drawn carriages by June 2028, moving to end a nearly 170-year tradition after the death of a teenager in Central Park and prompting threats of legal action from carriage drivers. The council voted 40-7, with two abstentions, to approve Romanch's Law, named after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died in June after being thrown from a runaway carriage in Central Park. The legislation would phase out the industry by June 1, 2028, while requiring Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration to develop a transition program for more than 150 active carriage drivers and other workers. The plan would include job training, career counseling and employment referrals, although financial compensation is not guaranteed. MAMDANI PRAISED OVER MOVE TO DISMANTLE CONTROVERSIAL NYC INDUSTRY — BUT INSIDERS SAY THERE’S MORE TO THE STORY President Donald Trump weighed in on the decision Thursday, criticizing the move to eliminate one of New York City's longtime tourist attractions. "The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience. So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!" he wrote on Truth Social. The Transport Workers Union (TWU), which represents carriage industry workers, threatened to challenge the ban in federal court and seek a temporary restraining order. Union representatives accused City Council Speaker Julie Menin of failing to adequately consult drivers whose livelihoods are at stake. MAN KILLED AFTER HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE BOLTS AND FLIPS NEAR POPULAR NEW YORK CITY TOURIST DESTINATION Opponents argued the city had failed to establish a concrete financial plan for drivers and carriage owners. An effort to delay the phaseout until January 2030 failed before the final vote. Menin defended the legislation Thursday, saying the council had strengthened worker protections and was prepared for a legal fight. "We're very confident in the legislation. That's why we took the time to work over the summer on the legislation," she said at a news conference. "We made changes to legislation to beef up worker protection. We are very confident in defending this law and will vigorously defend it. I've already talked to Steve Banks about it and our team, and we will vigorously defend this law." Animal rights group PETA also celebrated the vote, pledging $50,000 to help carriage horses retire as the industry winds down. The Central Park Conservancy celebrated the decision, arguing that horse-drawn carriages pose growing safety risks in a park that welcomes roughly 40 million visits annually. MAMDANI, CITY COUNCIL MOVE TO END ICONIC NYC HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE INDUSTRY AS WORKERS FACE UNCERTAIN FUTURE "In the modern era, carriages pose a serious — and even fatal — safety risk to park visitors, carriage drivers and the horses themselves. Our hearts break for the family of Romanch Mahajan, who stepped into a carriage earlier this summer and never thought he might lose his life," the organization wrote in a press release. The Conservancy said Mahajan's death was the ninth carriage-related incident in just over a year. The legislation also includes protections intended to prevent retired carriage horses from being sold for slaughter, while allowing owners to keep their animals. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The bill now heads to Mamdani, who has expressed support for ending the industry. If signed, it would bring an end to a decades-long political battle over one of New York City's most recognizable tourist attractions.

articles.title: DHS watchdog refers its Corey Lewandowski investigation to Justice Department for review
articles.summary: Lewandowski, the first manager on Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, was a top aide to then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem before she was fired.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security inspector general has referred its investigation of former “special government employee” Corey Lewandowski to the Justice Department, according to a person familiar with the investigation. The DHS investigation stems from questions about how a $220 million contract for an advertising campaign featuring then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem was awarded. At his Senate confirmation hearing, now-Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin testified in March that the department’s inspector general was looking into the contract. That investigation then expanded, according to a source familiar with the matter, after NBC News reported that Lewandowski was alleged to have sought payment in exchange for protecting and growing the interests of a company, the GEO Group, that was seeking government contracts unrelated to the ad campaign. In response to an inquiry from NBC News, Adam Trigg, an attorney for Lewandowski, said Thursday, “Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity.” The Wall Street Journal was first to report that the allegations are under review by the Justice Department. Sources previously described to NBC News two meetings with the GEO Group at which Lewandowski asked the company to pay him, with one source saying he wanted a “success fee.” The GEO Group declined his requests. A spokesperson for Lewandowski in March denied that account of his interactions with the GEO Group. “This is absolutely false and did not happen — Mr. Lewandowski never demanded any payment or compensation from the Geo Group, at any time,” his representative said. Before President Donald Trump fired her, Noem publicly admitted that she had personally approved the pricey contracts for the ad campaign but said Trump was aware of her involvement in their approval. After Noem was ousted, Trump told NBC News: “I wasn’t thrilled with it. I spent less money than that to become president. I didn’t know about it.” Lewandowski was a top aide to Noem who departed from DHS after she left. Reporting about allegations that Lewandowski requested payment from companies with business before DHS emerged only after Noem was fired and after Lewandowski, who was previously a top Trump adviser and the first manager of his 2016 campaign, left the department. Weeks before she was fired, Noem also faced scrutiny for her attempts to procure a $70 million luxury jet for the department she led. Asked about the referral of Lewandowski’s case to the Justice Department, Trump said Thursday: “I heard something about it, but I don’t know exactly what it is. All I know is I want my people to be honest, and if they’re not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted.” “I will never do anything to stop the prosecution of someone who’s dishonest,” he added.

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg's creative plan to pay California’s proposed billionaire tax without losing control of Meta | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A newly launched stock class being offered was partially engineered to help Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg pay the "billionaire's tax," should the measure be voted into law.
articles.body:
During Meta’s earnings call on Wednesday, the company revealed its board had approved a new class of non-voting stock, called Class C common stock. The shares give the holder an ownership stake but no vote on company decisions. This class takes effect in January. Meta says it will use the stock for capital raising, employee pay, and acquisitions — including its expensive push into AI — while maintaining the current voting structure that favors its founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, who controls around 60% of the vote.

Now, however, the New York Times has reported there’s another reason for the new class: helping Zuckerberg pay for California’s proposed “billionaire tax,” if voters approve it. Because the new shares carry no votes, he could sell some of them to cover the tax without giving up voting control.

Proposition 40 , which was drafted by Berkeley tax law professors and is being sponsored by California’s largest healthcare union (SEIU United Healthcare Workers West), would level a one-time 5% wealth tax on the net worth of several hundred California billionaires who primarily live in the state. Backers say the policy could generate as much as $100 billion over five years, the bulk of which would be used to pay for the state’s healthcare needs, with the rest for food assistance and education.

The Times also reports that Zuckerberg pressed Meta’s board to come up with a plan to protect him from the tax. According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm. Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes.

The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing made by Meta, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class.

The filing says that as far back as July, Zuckerberg was discussing the billionaire tax with board members. The topic came up again in additional meetings and communications throughout that month and August.

The filing also describes how the plan would work. Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own. The company calls this a one-time stock dividend and says it should work out to a two-for-one stock split. The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says.

That is where Prop 40 comes in. The filing says the dividend “will allow Mr. Zuckerberg to immediately sell or transfer up to 20% of the shares of Class C common stock that he receives in the Dividend, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the Company, for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control.” Because the dividend is one-for-one, half of his post-dividend shares will be Class C, so the 20% cap equals 10% of his total economic stake.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr. Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr. Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.”

It’s been estimated that Zuckerberg would have to pay as much as $11 billion as part of the tax.

Prop 40 has notably riled many of Silicon Valley’s most prominent businesspeople. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it. Other business leaders and critics of the proposal have criticized it online, with many claiming that it amounts to economic suicide for California, driving a capital flight from the state. However, as Meta’s new policy would appear to show, the state’s mega-companies and the people who run them have creative ways of dealing with the tax, should it materialize.

“Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S. Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added.

articles.title: Blanche says DOJ could block election certification in ‘doomsday scenario’
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche left the door open on whether the Justice Department (DOJ) would intervene in states’ midterm election verification processes, telling reporters Thursday there are hypothetical “scenarios” in which it could block the certification of votes. “Yes, of course there’s scenarios that we can all come up with hypothetically, you know, some doomsday…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche left the door open on whether the Justice Department (DOJ) would intervene in states’ midterm election verification processes, telling reporters Thursday there are hypothetical “scenarios” in which it could block the certification of votes.

“Yes, of course there’s scenarios that we can all come up with hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario for example, right?” he said. “So I don’t think it’s proper to make any kind of conclusory statements about what’s going to happen in the future, because I have no idea what’s happening in the future.”

Blanche added the DOJ has no intention “to improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.”

“There’s no circumstances that we would ever do that,” he continued. “Of course I’m not going to say that. But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not, no, not at all.”

Blanche said earlier this month the DOJ plans to send 1,000 election monitors to polling places in every state on Election Day. At the time, he told Fox News anchor Shannon Bream the department’s presence would serve to ensure federal law is properly enforced, adding the government has been monitoring elections since the 1960s.

During the Fox interview, Blanche went on to accuse Democrats of “fearmongering” by claiming the DOJ is trying to intimidate voters.

On Tuesday, Democratic leaders and election groups filed a lawsuit against President Trump and the DOJ, accusing the administration of “ threats and intimidation ” ahead of Election Day — pointing to its efforts to push states to identify and remove suspected non-U.S. citizens from voter rolls and threats of criminal prosecution against election officials who refuse to comply.

DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told The Washington Post Wednesday that “ensuring that only eligible citizens vote and that every lawful ballot is counted a requirement of federal law.”

The lawsuit specifically cites the DOJ’s demand to California officials to set aside ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) identified as noncitizens. It also alleged the administration’s threat to imprison state and local election officials violated the Voting Rights Act.

The DOJ sued the Golden State last week after giving its officials 48 hours to compare the 20,000-name DHS list to California’s the voter rolls. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) slammed the lawsuit, saying his state’s elections “are NOT Donald Trump’s to control.”

On Monday, the DOJ announced 28 alleged non-U.S. citizens in California were charged in connection with illegally voting. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said all of the 28 “defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week.”

Trump, who has long held immigration as a central issue over both of his presidencies, has frequently made unsubstantiated claims surrounding non-citizens voting in U.S. elections and alleged the practice plays a role in voter fraud in Democratic states.
